structured_output.title: A base like /admin/ now matches only whole path segments, not any path that starts with the same letters
structured_output.premise: A Nuxt app with baseURL '/admin/' has a page at '/admin-dashboard' (nuxt/nuxt#33924). ufo's withoutBase only checked startsWith, so it treated '/admin' in '/admin-dashboard' as the base and returned '/-dashboard', which breaks routing. withBase had the mirror bug: it decided '/admin-dashboard' already had the base and returned it without prefixing, so the link never got '/admin/' in front.
structured_output.verdict: withBase and withoutBase now treat the base as present only when '/', '?' or the end of the string follows it. Evidence: four tests that failed before now pass, and all earlier cases still pass. Risk: '#' is not a boundary, so inputs like '/admin#top' now behave differently with no test, and callers relying on the old loose prefix match will see different output.

chapters.title: withoutBase stops cutting '/admin' out of '/admin-dashboard'
chapters.before: withoutBase('/admin-dashboard', '/admin/') and with base '/admin' both returned '/-dashboard', so the assertions failed.
chapters.after: Both calls return '/admin-dashboard' unchanged. '/admin/admin-dashboard' still becomes '/admin-dashboard' and '/admin/dashboard' still becomes '/dashboard'.
facts: The base is normalised by withoutTrailingSlash, so '/admin/' and '/admin' act the same and both become '/admin'.
In '/admin-dashboard' the character after '/admin' is '-', so the new guard at lines 327-330 returns the input untouched.
With '/admin/admin-dashboard' the next character is '/', so the slice still runs and gives '/admin-dashboard' (trace line 226).

Only '/', '?' and the end of the string count as boundaries. '#' does not, so withoutBase('/admin#x', '/admin') would now return the input unchanged, where it used to return '/#x'. No test covers this.

open_questions.question: withBase uses the same startsWith check. Does it make the same mistake in the other direction?
Do the real boundary cases, such as the query form '/api?test' and the exact match '/base', still have their base stripped?

chapters.title: withBase now adds '/admin' in front of '/admin-dashboard' instead of treating it as already based
chapters.before: withBase('/admin-dashboard', '/admin/' or '/admin') returned '/admin-dashboard' unchanged, so the test expecting '/admin/admin-dashboard' failed.
chapters.after: The guard rejects '-' as a boundary, so execution falls through to joinURL('/admin', '/admin-dashboard'), which returns '/admin/admin-dashboard'.
facts: Only the head run calls joinURL here (trace lines 77-82 and 99-104), and it produces '/admin/admin-dashboard'.
Inputs already under the base, '/admin/admin-dashboard' and '/admin/dashboard', still come back unchanged because the next character is '/'.
withBase('/admin#x', '/admin') would now give '/admin/admin#x' because '#' is not accepted as a boundary. No test covers this.

open_questions.question: Do the older withBase cases, such as an exact match, an empty input or a full URL, still come back the same?

answers.answer: Yes. Before the change, withBase saw '/admin-dashboard' as already having the base and returned it unprefixed. Now it falls through to joinURL and returns '/admin/admin-dashboard'.

chapters.title: withoutBase still strips the base at real boundaries, including before a query
chapters.before: '/api?test' with base '/api' gave '/?test', '/base' with base '/base/' gave '/', and '/base/a' gave '/a'.
chapters.after: The same outputs come back: '/?test', '/', '/a'. Inputs that don't match the base, and full URLs, are returned unchanged.
facts: '?' counts as a boundary, so '/api?test' still becomes '/?test' (trace line 196).
When the input ends exactly at the base, nextChar is undefined, so '/base/a' with base '/base/a/' still gives '/'.
Base '/' still returns early through isEmptyURL and never reaches the new guard.

answers.answer: Yes. '/api?test' still gives '/?test', and the exact match '/base' still gives '/', because '?' and the end of the string both count as boundaries.

chapters.title: withBase keeps every earlier result the same
chapters.before: '/base' and '/base/a' with base '/base/' came back unchanged, '' with base '/foo' gave '/foo', and 'https://test.com' passed through untouched.
chapters.after: Identical outputs: the next character is the end of the string or '/', and full URLs exit early through hasProtocol.
facts: '/base/' with base '/base' passes because nextChar is '/'. '/base' with base '/base/' passes because nextChar is undefined.
None of these cases puts '?' right after the base in withBase. That path is accepted only because the code says so.

answers.answer: Yes. All ten original withBase cases return the same values on both sides of the change.
